extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics students, philosophers of mathematics, and general readers interested in the nature of mathematical practice
extracted.subtask_description: Sketching an archetype of the 'ideal mathematician' to expose the epistemic, social, and communicative standards by which mathematical work is judged (proof, rigor, existence, publication practice, audience, and applicability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith in rigorous proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The mathematician "rests his faith on rigorous proof; he believes that the difference between a correct proof and an incorrect one is an unmistakable and decisive difference."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigor is treated as the foundational standard of correctness. However, the text notes a paradox: mathematicians often "can give no coherent explanation of what is meant by rigor," and the line between complete and incomplete proof can be "somewhat fuzzy, and often controversial." Use of 'rigor' functions as both an ideal standard and a social marker rather than always a precisely defined procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as convincing the knowledgeable audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "Well, it’s an argument that convinces someone who knows the subject." (A proof is judged by its ability to convince domain experts.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical criterion: a proof's adequacy is measured by whether it convinces those familiar with the subculture and standard arguments. This makes proof partly audience-relative; the page emphasizes that formalization exists in principle but that the working definition is about convincing competent readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal proof versus practical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal proofs (axiomatize theory, transform formulas by rules of logic) exist as an ideal, but "no one ever really does it" because it "would take forever."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While formalization shows in-principle correctness, actual mathematical practice relies on informal, higher-level arguments and shared conventions. Evaluations should acknowledge the distinction: formalizability is a theoretical guarantee, not the everyday method of working mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence as model/consistency (operational existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians treat objects (e.g., 'non-Riemannian hypersquares') as existing because "the axioms for a hypersquare possess a model... no formal contradiction can be deduced from them," and so one is "free to postulate their existence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The operational criterion for 'existence' in mathematics is model-theoretic/consistency-based: existence is established by proving a model (or consistency) rather than by empirical observation. Evaluations of claims about existence should consider whether an axiomatic system admits a model or whether existence is only an informal assertion within a subculture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and communicability to non-initiates
rubrics_metrics.description: The work "is intelligible only to a small group of specialists" and attempts to explain to outsiders often fail: definitions can be "so recondite as to defeat all attempts at comprehension."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A criterion for exposition is whether the work can be framed so non-specialists can grasp at least the general nature and purpose; lack of accessibility is an expected trait but also a communicative deficit. Examples include the press-release dialogue where the mathematician resists simplification and the apprentice requirement of several years to understand the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication convention: concealment of human processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Published writings "pile up formalism... Three pages of definitions are followed by seven lemmas and, finally, a theorem..." and the writing "follows an unbreakable convention: to conceal any sign that the author or the intended reader is a human being."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgments of written work should account for this convention: formal presentations are designed to appear mechanically derived from definitions, but understanding often depends on tacit knowledge (motivations, standard arguments). Reviewers/readers must decode lemmas to find the new idea; the publication's apparent completeness can mask dependence on subcultural context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social markers of identity and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: The mathematician "is labeled by his field, by how much he publishes, and especially by whose work he uses, and by whose taste he follows in his choice of problems."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Status and evaluation in mathematics are influenced by field affiliation, publication record, intellectual lineage (whose work you use), and choice of problems (whose taste you follow). These sociological criteria matter in judging a mathematician's work and career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem selection and prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Conferences center on canonical problems ("the decision problem", "the construction problem") often because they were stated by a founding figure; such problems acquire prestige and attract the best workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige of problems is partly historical and social (linked to founders and partial solutions). Evaluations of importance may therefore consider whether an effort addresses a recognized central problem with established prestige in the subfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding 'debasement' in public communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal mathematician resists public-relations simplifications: he wants public sympathy and support "but not if it means debasing myself... getting involved in public relations gimmicks."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a normative stance, communicating to the public should not involve oversimplification that misrepresents the work. This is a criterion for public-facing exposition: preserve integrity rather than trade clarity for popularity, though the text illustrates tensions (press officer dialogue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability, analyzability, and predictive value (physicist's criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the physicist's/model-theory perspective: a model should "describe certain phenomena fairly accurately," be "analyzable," and have "predictive value"—otherwise it has little significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For work intended to model physical phenomena, evaluation emphasizes analyzability and predictive power over abstract elegance. The physicist interviewed replaces 'beautiful' with 'analyzable' and prizes models that yield testable consequences and guide experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of experiment and computation depending on goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical computation can replace experiment for technological/production problems but not for pure science, where "the elimination of experimentation is a contradiction in terms."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of computational approaches should consider context: for technology and engineering, computer experiments may be appropriate; for fundamental science, empirical experimentation remains indispensable. The sufficiency of computation is judged by whether it can produce reliable, explainable consequences and is not so complex as to preclude reasoned derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition as stored experience but fallible
rubrics_metrics.description: "Intuition is an expression of experience. Stored experience... To what extent can one be deceived by intuition? 'This occurs not infrequently.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intuition as a heuristic rooted in experience, but treat it as fallible. Evaluations guided by intuition should be corroborated by analyzable reasoning or empirical checks when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as a provisional/model-based enterprise (model-theory stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the interviewed physicist: mathematics and physical theories are 'models'—provisional constructs whose worth lies in how good (useful, analyzable, predictive) they are, not in absolute indubitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating mathematical contributions to science, prefer assessments that foreground utility as a model (descriptive/predictive success) rather than metaphysical claims of absolute truth. This offers an alternative rubric to strict Platonist standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and gatekeeping as evaluative mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Graduate study and apprenticeship absorb the way of thinking; those who cannot 'absorb our way of thinking' are flunked, and dissenters are labeled 'crank' or 'misfit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment often relies on whether a person can internalize community standards via training. This functions as both a quality-control mechanism and a gatekeeping criterion; evaluators should be aware of its sociological role and possible exclusionary effects.
